column2: If the enemy is strong, bent on conquest by adharma and sinful in resolve, one should make peace with him by holding oneself back.
Or, leaving the capital, one may cross the calamity by some other means; and if that is so, preserving one's wealth, one may earn it again.
But as for what could be done by mere sacrifice, with the power to cross the calamity, what knower of artha and dharma would give up his very self beyond that?
One should be disgusted by confinement; what pity is there for an enemy's wealth? But the self must never be given up, so long as it is possible to avoid it.
[Yudhishthira said:] "When there is rage within, pressure from without, the treasury is spent and the counsel is leaked, what is left to be done?"
Slain, he ascends to heaven; victorious, he dwells on earth; giving up his life in battle, he attains the world of Shakra.
Having secured access to all the worlds, he may turn to gentleness and show humility out of trust, or else resolve upon his sandals (and flight).
Or he may wish to withdraw and, as he pleases, conciliate; having signalled to a friend, he should then set forth himself.
[Yudhishthira said:] "By what may a brahmana live when a base time has come, without abandoning his sons and grandsons out of compassion, grandsire?"
[Bhishma said:] "Relying on the strength of knowledge one must live when matters have come to that; all this is for a good end, nothing at all is for a bad end.
He who takes from the wicked and gives to the good, making himself the means of transfer, is a knower of all dharma.
Without unsettling his standing in the kingdom through his own great anger, king, he may take even what is not given, from the giver's wealth, thinking 'it is mine.'
One who, purified by the strength of knowledge, behaves even in ways that are blamed, a wise man who knows conduct: what can you say to him?
Those whose livelihood is made by strength do not like the ways of others; the strong, Yudhishthira, grow by their own energy.
The scripture that one finds laid down without distinction, that the middling follow, and the intelligent follow what is higher still.
One should not torment officiating priests, household priests and teachers who have been honoured with courtesies, nor brahmanas; whoever torments them incurs fault.
This is not the conduct of the good, slander and backbiting; the good, Yudhishthira, are speakers only of merits among the good.
As two well-matched, well-tamed, good draught-animals bear a yoke by lifting it, so should a king act; and as helpers come to him while he bears the load, so do others also.
Others hold conduct alone to be the weightier mark of dharma; those fond of Shankha and Likhita do not wish it so; out of softness or greed they might say such a word.
Here they see even the seers' precedent for the livelihood of one in wrongful action; yet nowhere is there any authority equal to the seers'.
Even the gods punish the lowest of men who stands in wrongful action; one who gains wealth by deceit falls away from dharma.
The dharma that is honoured on every side by the good, for the causes of prosperity, and approved by the heart, that is the dharma one resolves upon.
He who knows dharma endowed with four qualities is a knower of dharma; like a snake's, the track of dharma is hard to seek.
As a hunter follows the track of a wounded deer by the drops of blood at its flank, so should one follow the track of dharma.
In this way, imperishable one, one must go by the path trodden by the good; know this as the conduct of royal sages, Yudhishthira."
Therefore he should generate a treasury, gathering and protecting it; having protected it, he should show favour; this is eternal dharma.
A treasury is not born of pure scrupulousness, nor of cruelty; resorting to the middle course, one should gather a treasury.
How can the weak have a treasury? How can one without a treasury have strength? How can the weak have a kingdom? How can one without a kingdom have fortune?
For one who lives on high, the loss of fortune is like death; therefore a king should increase his treasury, strength and friends.
People look down on a king whose treasury is depleted; they are not pleased with his little, yet they bestir themselves over his business.
By reason of fortune a king gains the highest honour; it hides his sins as a garment hides what is private in a woman.
People he formerly wronged follow his prosperity, like jackals and wolves ever intent on killing; how can such a king have happiness, best of the Bharatas?
One should exert oneself and not despair, for exertion is manliness; even at a place without a joint one may break, but one should never bow before anyone here.
One might even take shelter in the forest and roam with bands of robbers, but should not roam with robbers who have broken all limits; the armies of robbers are easy to find for cruel deeds, Bharata.
For everyone is alarmed by one without limits; even robbers are suspicious of those who act without mercy.
He should establish a limit that gladdens people's minds; even a small limit becomes honoured in the world.
A man resolved that "there is no this world and no other" is not to be trusted; one cannot place trust in an unbeliever who is timid and full of suspicion.
As taking from the good is one thing, so non-harm is another among robbers; beings grow attached to robbers who keep their limits.

Killing one who is not fighting, molesting women, ingratitude, seizing the property of a knower of Brahman, leaving nothing remaining, theft from a woman, and persisting in these among robbers are condemned.
He who avoids these is the robber indeed; those who do not plot the ruin of such a one, though they reproach him, do not leave nothing remaining; this is certain.
Therefore, even when robbers are in command, something must be left remaining; one should not commit cruel acts thinking "I am strong."
Those who leave something remaining, dear, see something remaining everywhere; for those who leave nothing, fear is constant, because nothing is left.
Adharma, dharma: it is like a wolf's track; no one here has ever seen the fruits of dharma and adharma.
The strong would wish to be everything; all lies in the power of the strong; the strong man gains fortune, force and ministers here.
He who is not wealthy is fallen, and what little he has is a leftover; for the strong, much that is unwholesome is nothing, and nothing saves from fear.
Both hold sovereignty over truth, and both save from great fear; I think strength greater than dharma, for from strength dharma proceeds.
Dharma is founded on strength, as the moving is founded on the earth; as smoke follows the wind, dharma follows strength.

Dharma depends on strength in one who is powerless as a creeper on a tree; dharma is subject to the strong, as pleasure to the enjoyers; nothing is impossible for the strong, and for the strong all is pure.
The ill-conducted, weak in strength, hold to a measure; then the whole world is alarmed at him as at a wolf.
One cast down and despised lives a life of sorrow; a life that is slighted is like death.
One should enter the brahma-kshatra way, having done much that is very hard, not minding what the world says about it.
Blameless, with such conduct he soon becomes highly esteemed; he may enjoy happiness and wealth and protect them by this conduct; in this world he gains honour, and in the next a great fruit.
A smiter, wise, heroic, learned and merciful, guarding imperishable dharma, devoted to brahmanas and honouring his teachers.
Born of a Nishada woman to a kshatriya, keeping to the dharma of the kshatriya, a Nishada's son named Kapavya attained perfection though a robber.
In the forest, at evening and in the forenoon, he roused the herds of deer; he knew the ways of the deer kinds and was skilled in their watering-places.
Knowing every region of the forest, ever roaming Pariyatra, a knower of dharma toward all beings, of unerring arrows and firm weapons,
Single-handed he conquered armies of many hundreds; and in the great forest he honoured his aged, blind parents.
With honey, meat, roots, fruits and food of many kinds he honoured and fed them, and attended on them well.
Protecting the forest-dwelling brahmanas who had gone forth as ascetics, he would even bring them deer killed in the great forest.
To those who would not accept it, fearing a robber's food, he would leave it at their houses and go away at dawn.
As you tell us, so shall we do; protect us as is just, as a mother and as a father.
[Kapavya said:] "Do not kill a timid woman, nor a child, nor an ascetic; one who is not fighting is not to be slain, nor are women to be seized by force.
A woman is by no means to be killed by one who fights among all beings; always one must fight for the welfare of cows and brahmanas, and for their sake.
Crops must not be destroyed, nor the plough obstructed, where gods, ancestors and guests are honoured.
Among all beings a brahmana deserves release, and honour must be paid to them even with all one's wealth.
For the man whose brahmanas, enraged, counsel his defeat, there is no protector in the three worlds.
He who insults brahmanas or desires their ruin meets a sure downfall, as surely as the sun rises.
Sitting here, one looks for the fruit hereafter according to one's ability; whoever will not give to us, against each of them we shall march with the force.
Punishment is ordained for the sake of discipline, not for killing; for those who harass the disciplined, their slaying is declared to be dharma.
Those who make a living by obstructing the realm are inferred from that, like worms on a corpse.
But robbers here who would live by the dharmashastra, even they, though robbers, would soon attain success."
[Bhishma said:] "They all carried out Kapavya's instruction, found a livelihood, and ceased from sin.
By that deed Kapavya attained great perfection, practising the welfare of the good and turning robbers away from sin.
He who ever recounts this deed of Kapavya will never meet fear from the beings of the forest.
He has no fear from mortals, nor in any way from immortals, king; neither from the good nor the bad; he is indeed a protector in the forests."
That would be for his strength or for sacrifice; plants not fit to be enjoyed, once cut and cooked, become fit to be enjoyed.
He who worships with oblations neither gods, nor ancestors, nor men, the knowers of the Veda call such wealth calamitous.
A righteous lord of the earth should seize that wealth, king; such wealth would please neither the people nor the treasury.
He who takes from the wicked and gives to the good, making himself the means of transfer, I think is a knower of dharma.
Some creatures are born of sprouts, and are spoken of fittingly; they come into being even unwished for; so sacrifice is extended.
As with gnats and mosquitoes, and as with ants born of eggs, that same livelihood holds among the non-sacrificers; so dharma is ordained.
In a lake not very deep, three friends, fishes, Kaunteya, lived as companions among abundant fish.
Among those three water-dwellers one knew the right moment, another was far-sighted, and one was a procrastinator.
Once the fishermen drained that water on every side, through various channels into the low places.
Seeing the lake draining at the coming of danger, the far-sighted one spoke then to the two friends.

This calamity has arisen for all dwellers in the water; let us go quickly elsewhere while the path is not yet blocked.
mahabharata:12:135.7	He who by sound policy wards off a harm before it comes does not meet doubt; if it pleases you both, let us go.
But the procrastinator among them said, "It is well said, but there need be no haste yet; so is my resolve."
Then the ready-witted one said to the far-sighted one, "When the time comes, nothing will be lost to me, by right means."
Then seeing that body of water draining, the fishermen bound the fish by various devices.
While the pond was being stirred, with its water flowing out, the procrastinator was caught together with the others.
Seeing the net being drawn on the fish with ropes, the ready-witted one slipped in among the others and held on.
Having clamped on to that very net, he stayed just so; and they took all of them there to be tied up.
Then, when the fish were being washed in the clear water, the ready-witted one let go of the rope and was quickly freed.
But the procrastinator, dull-minded, poor in sense and unaware, met his death, deluded, like one whose senses are injured.
So whoever through delusion does not wake to the arrival of the time perishes quickly, like the procrastinating fish.
The man who does nothing good at the outset, thinking "I am clever," meets doubt, like the ready-witted fish.
But the man who makes provision for the future, doing what is fitting, gains the highest good, like the far-sighted fish.
Kalas, kashthas, muhurtas, days, nadis, kshanas, lavas, fortnights, months, seasons and years alike,
Place is spoken of as a region of the earth, and time is not seen; for the accomplishment of the intended aim, by right means, and so too of what is so.
These two are declared by the sages in the shastras of dharma and artha and the shastras of liberation to be chief, and are accepted among men by the lords of desire.
One who acts after examining, and is diligent, should accomplish things properly; by place and time as intended, he would gain the fruit.
[Yudhishthira said:] "So I wish to hear the supreme wisdom, best of the Bharatas, so that a king, surrounded by enemies, may not be bewildered.
Skilled in dharma and artha, wise, versed in all the shastras, I ask you, best of the Kurus; you should explain it to me.
How should a king act when seized by many enemies? I wish to hear all this in due order.
Enemies, the obstructors, though many, strive to uproot a king in distress, as one already scorched by them.
How can a weak and lone man without allies, sought on all sides by the very mighty, hold his ground?
How would he find a friend and an enemy, bull of the Bharatas? And how should he act between the enemy and the friend?
When an enemy of known marks has turned friend, king, what should a man do, or what having done will he be happy?
With whom should he make war, or with whom ally, and how should a weak man live amid enemies?
Except from Bhishma, Shantanu's son, truthful and master of his senses, seek this out, mighty-armed, and tell me all."
[Bhishma said:] "This question of yours, Yudhishthira, is fitting, a source of virtues; hear from me in full, son, the secret in calamities, Bharata.
An enemy becomes a friend and a friend turns hostile, through the conjunction of capability in affairs; for the course of events always follows that.
Therefore one should trust and also wage war, knowing place and time, in deciding what should and should not be done.
The wise should always make alliances, and those seeking their welfare should resolve; even with enemies peace should be made; lives must be protected, Bharata.
The unwise man who never allies with enemies would gain no profit and no fruits, Bharata.
But he who allies with an enemy and quarrels with a friend, seeing the logic of interest, gains a very great fruit.
Here they cite this ancient tale, the dialogue of a cat and a mouse in a banyan tree.
In a certain great forest stood a huge banyan, covered with a net of creepers and filled with many flocks of birds.
Trunked, cloud-like, cool-shaded and delightful, it grew at the edge of Vairantya, crowded with beasts of prey and deer.
At its root, having made a hole with a hundred mouths, lived a very wise mouse named Palita.
And in its branches lived happily a cat named Lomasha, destroyer of birds and creatures.
There a chandala who had made his hut at Vairantya set a snare each day at sundown.
There, having laid sinew snares properly, he went home, slept well, and came back at dawn.
There each night many kinds of animals were caught; and once the cat, though careful, was caught.
When that natural enemy, ever an attacker, was bound, the wise Palita, knowing the moment, roamed quite fearless.
Moving about in that forest, trusting and seeking food, he soon saw meat.
He climbed on that trap and ate the meat, laughing in his mind at his bound enemy above him.
Engrossed in the meat, looking about, he once saw another terrible enemy of his arrived.
It was a mongoose named Harika, lying in a hole in the ground, the colour of reed-blossom, restless, with red eyes.
Drawn by the mouse's scent it came swiftly, licking its mouth, standing with its face upward on the ground.
And on a branch he saw another enemy, an owl named Chandraka, sharp-beaked, a night-roamer, dwelling in a hollow.
When he had come within range of the mongoose and the owl, this thought came to him, having met great fear.
In this very painful calamity, with death at hand and fear arisen on all sides, what should a well-wisher do?
Thus hemmed in on every side, seeing the same everywhere, he was fear-stricken, and made this final resolve.

Calamity is mostly destruction; life is but one in a hundred; this danger has come upon us, doubtful on every side.

mahabharata:12:136.38	But a wise one like me should not fall into bewilderment; I shall strive for life as long as breath is held.
mahabharata:12:136.39	For the wise, endowed with intellect and skilled in the science of policy, do not panic on meeting calamity, nor on gaining great goals.
mahabharata:12:136.40	I see now no refuge here but the cat; this creature is in distress, and I have great business with him.
mahabharata:12:136.41	How, desiring life, can I stand now, sought by three enemies? Therefore I take refuge in this enemy, the cat.
mahabharata:12:136.42	Resorting to the science of the kshatriyas I contemplate his good, by which I shall deceive this host of enemies with intention.
mahabharata:12:136.43	He is my extreme enemy, come to utter distress; if the fool can be made to grasp his own interest through an alliance...
mahabharata:12:136.44	Sometimes, falling into trouble, he might make peace with me; the teachers say that even an enemy settled with a stronger one should be accepted, by one seeking life in distress.
mahabharata:12:136.45	A wise enemy is better than a foolish friend; my life rests on this enemy, the cat.
mahabharata:12:136.46	Well, I shall speak to him, a reason for protecting myself; may this enemy now become wise through alliance.
Then, knowing the truth of interest, and the times for peace and war, the mouse spoke to the cat these words, preceded by conciliation.

I speak to you in friendship: cat, are you alive? I wish for your life; our good is common.
mahabharata:12:136.49	Gentle one, do not despair; you will live as before. I shall deliver you, and would give up my life for you.
mahabharata:12:136.50	There is a plentiful means here that occurs to me, by which you can win release, and I the good.
[Bhishma said:] Then they went as they had come: Death, Kala and the serpent; Arjunaka became free of anger, and Gautami free of sorrow.
Avikshit, the righteous-souled, was equal to Indra in valour, devoted to sacrifice, delighting in rites, steadfast and self-controlled.
Great gifts have been given, and shraddhas again and again; my age is far advanced, son, and merit has been stored as I could; this Gandhari, whose sons are slain, waits for me with fortitude.
Having said this, enraged, he rushed with a sword near Keshava and cut off the head of Kritavarman.
[Yudhishthira said:] "They say that abandoning a devotee is exceedingly sinful, equal in the world to killing a brahmana; therefore I shall never abandon him for my own comfort, Mahendra."
Tormented by the intense stench, he said to the divine messenger, "Go, good sir, to those whose messenger you are; go to them nearby."
